questions.question: How do you reverse a String in Java?
questions.title: Reverse a String
questions.direct_answer: Use StringBuilder's reverse() method for simplicity and performance, or manually iterate the string backwards building a new string. StringBuilder is preferred because it's mutable and avoids creating multiple intermediate String objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of String immutability and knowledge of StringBuilder as the proper tool for string manipulation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to modify a String in place (impossible due to immutability) or using inefficient string concatenation in a loop
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate both the StringBuilder approach and manual iteration, explain why StringBuilder is O(n) while string concatenation would be O(n²), and mention when you'd use each

sections.title: String Reversal in Java
sections.content:
Reversing a string in Java requires working around **String immutability** — once created, a String object cannot be changed. The most efficient approach uses **StringBuilder**, a mutable character sequence designed for string manipulation. Think of StringBuilder like a text editor where you can change content directly, while String is like a printed document where any change requires printing a new copy. For a production Java app processing user input, StringBuilder's reverse() method provides O(n) time complexity with minimal memory overhead. Manual iteration (reading characters backwards into a new structure) works too but requires more code. Understanding this distinction separates developers who grasp Java's memory model from those who treat strings like character arrays.

The key insight: **every string concatenation creates a new object**, so reversing with + in a loop creates n temporary objects, turning an O(n) operation into O(n²) disaster.

sections.title: Reverse a String at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Easiest|~one-liner|new StringBuilder(s).reverse()|then toString()|interview-safe
blue|Manual|~two-pointer swap|swap ends moving inward|on a char[] (toCharArray)|O(n) time, O(n) space
emerald|Why ask|~tests the basics|loops and char[]|immutability awareness|edge: empty / null
rose|Watch out|~Unicode|surrogate pairs / emoji|naive reverse corrupts them|mention it if asked

sections.title: Reversing Strings with StringBuilder and Manual Iteration
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **StringBuilder.reverse()** for production code — it's one line, tested by millions of applications, and optimized by the JVM. This is your default choice when reversing user input in a report generator or validating palindrome passwords.

Use **manual iteration** when you need to understand the mechanics during interviews or when reversing only part of a string (like reversing words individually in a sentence).

Use the **char array swap** approach when working with character-level algorithms or when the interviewer explicitly asks for an in-place solution. For most Java backend scenarios processing form data or generating formatted output, StringBuilder.reverse() is the professional choice that balances readability and performance.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **String Concatenation in Loop**: Freshers often write String result = ""; then result += charAt(i) in a loop, creating n new String objects and causing O(n²) time complexity instead of O(n). Each += creates a new String because of immutability.
- **Ignoring Null Safety**: Calling reverse() on null input throws NullPointerException, but many freshers forget the null check, causing production crashes on empty form fields.
- **Using StringBuffer Instead of StringBuilder**: StringBuffer is thread-safe but slower due to synchronization overhead — unnecessary for local variables where only one thread accesses the data, which is 99% of string reversal scenarios.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **String immutability**: Strings cannot be modified after creation, so any manipulation requires creating new objects
**StringBuilder.reverse()**: Most efficient approach, O(n) time and space, single method call, preferred for production code
**Manual iteration**: Iterate from length-1 to 0, appending characters to StringBuilder, useful for understanding mechanics
**Performance trap**: String concatenation with + in a loop is O(n²) due to creating n intermediate String objects
**char array swap**: Convert to char[], swap elements in place with two pointers, then construct new String from array
**Null handling**: Always check for null or empty strings before reversal to prevent NullPointerException in production
**StringBuffer vs StringBuilder**: StringBuffer is synchronized (thread-safe but slower), StringBuilder is unsynchronized (faster for single-threaded use)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The best way to reverse a string in Java is using StringBuilder's reverse method. You create a StringBuilder from the input string, call reverse on it, and convert back to String with toString. That's it — one line that runs in linear time. The reason we need StringBuilder is because Strings in Java are immutable. Once created, you can't change them. So if you tried reversing with string concatenation in a loop, like building the result with the plus operator, you'd actually create a new String object on every iteration. That turns your algorithm from O of n into O of n squared, which is terrible for large strings. For example, if you're processing user comments in a report generator, reversing a thousand-character string with concatenation would create a thousand temporary objects. The manual approach is to iterate backwards through the original string, from the last index to zero, appending each character to a new StringBuilder. That works fine and helps you understand what's happening under the hood, but in production code, just use the built-in reverse method. One gotcha freshers miss: always check if the input is null or empty before calling reverse, or you'll get a NullPointerException when processing empty form fields. In an interview, I'd show both the StringBuilder approach and explain why string concatenation fails, which demonstrates I understand Java's memory model.

questions.question: How do you count the frequency of each character in a String?
questions.title: Character Frequency Count
questions.direct_answer: Use a HashMap with Character keys and Integer values to store frequencies. Iterate through the string, and for each character, increment its count using getOrDefault or merge. For only lowercase English letters, an int array of size 26 is more space-efficient.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to use HashMap for frequency counting and understanding of when an array solution is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a primitive array without considering Unicode or special characters, or writing verbose HashMap updates instead of using getOrDefault or merge
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both HashMap and array approaches, explain time-space trade-offs, and extend to finding the first non-repeating character using the same frequency map

sections.title: Character Frequency Counting with HashMap
sections.content:
Counting character frequencies is a classic **hash map problem** — you need to track how many times each unique character appears in a string. A **HashMap<Character, Integer>** stores each character as a key with its count as the value.

As you iterate through the string, you either insert a new entry with count 1 or increment an existing count. Java's **getOrDefault** method simplifies this: it returns the current count if the key exists, or a default value (0) if it doesn't, letting you write clean one-liners. For restricted character sets like lowercase a-z, an **int array of size 26** is more space-efficient — map 'a' to index 0, 'b' to index 1, and so on. This pattern appears constantly in backend applications: analyzing user search queries, detecting spam patterns in comments, or generating word clouds from report data. The HashMap approach handles all Unicode characters including emojis, while the array approach trades generality for speed and memory efficiency.

sections.title: Character Frequency Count at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Approach|~hash map count|Map<Character, Integer>|merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)|O(n) time
blue|Faster|~int[] for ASCII|int[256] tally|index by the char|no boxing
emerald|Output|~loop the entries|print char + count|sort if needed|TreeMap for ordering
rose|Edges|~case & spaces|normalize case?|ignore whitespace?|clarify with interviewer

sections.title: Character Frequency Counter with HashMap and Array
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use the **HashMap approach** for general text processing where the input can contain any Unicode characters — user comments, international names, emoji-filled social media posts. This is your default for real-world Java backend applications.

Use **Map.merge()** for cleaner code when inserting or updating — it handles the "key exists or not" logic automatically.

Use the **int array approach** when you know the character set is restricted, like processing DNA sequences (ACGT only), counting only letters in English text analysis, or solving LeetCode-style problems where constraints guarantee lowercase a-z. The array is faster (direct index access vs hash computation) and uses less memory (104 bytes vs HashMap overhead). In a user report generator, if you're counting letter frequencies for analytics, the array works perfectly; if you're analyzing arbitrary user input that might include punctuation and non-English characters, HashMap is essential.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Verbose HashMap Updates**: Freshers write if-else blocks checking containsKey before putting, like if map contains key then get and increment else put 1. This is 5 lines when getOrDefault does it in one line, showing unfamiliarity with HashMap methods.
- **Array Index Errors**: Using an int array without validating the character range causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when the input contains spaces, numbers, or special characters — freshers assume clean input but production data is messy.
- **Creating New Integer Objects**: Writing frequencyMap.put(c, new Integer(count)) instead of auto-boxing with just count, or worse, not knowing that Integer objects are immutable so you can't modify them directly.
- **Ignoring Case Sensitivity**: Not calling toLowerCase when the problem requires case-insensitive counting, so 'A' and 'a' are counted separately in a word frequency analyzer.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **HashMap<Character, Integer>**: Standard approach for counting character frequencies, handles all Unicode characters including emojis
**getOrDefault(key, 0)**: Returns existing count or 0 if key absent, enabling one-line increment without null checks
**Map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)**: Cleaner alternative that automatically handles insertion and increment in one method call
**int[26] array**: Space-efficient for lowercase English letters only, map character to index with char minus 'a'
**Time complexity**: O(n) for both approaches where n is string length, single pass through input string
**Space complexity**: O(k) for HashMap where k is unique characters, O(1) for fixed-size array regardless of input
**Case sensitivity**: Call toLowerCase() or toUpperCase() first if problem requires case-insensitive frequency counting

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd use a HashMap with Character keys and Integer values to count character frequencies. You iterate through the string once, and for each character, you check if it's already in the map. If it is, increment its count. If not, add it with count one. Java makes this really clean with the getOrDefault method — you write map dot put c comma map dot getOrDefault c comma zero plus one. That returns the current count if the key exists or zero if it doesn't, so you don't need separate if-else logic. There's also Map dot merge which is even cleaner for this pattern. Now, if the problem guarantees the input only contains lowercase English letters, you can optimize with an int array of size 26. You map 'a' to index zero, 'b' to index one, and so on using the character minus 'a' as the index. Then just iterate and increment the array at that position. This is faster because array access is direct while HashMap has to compute hash codes, but it only works for restricted character sets. The HashMap approach is safer for production code because user input can contain anything — spaces, punctuation, Unicode characters. A common mistake freshers make is writing verbose code checking if the map contains the key before putting, when getOrDefault does that automatically. Another is using the array approach without validating the character is actually a lowercase letter, which causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the first space or number. In an interview, I'd show both approaches and explain that HashMap is the general solution, but array is better when you know the constraints.

questions.question: How do you check if two Strings are anagrams?
questions.title: Anagram Check
questions.direct_answer: Two approaches: sort both strings using toCharArray and Arrays.sort, then compare with Arrays.equals; or count character frequencies in one string and decrement for the other, checking if all counts are zero. Both are O(n log n) for sorting and O(n) for frequency counting.

interviewer_intent.testing: Algorithm design skills and understanding of multiple solution approaches with trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not checking if lengths are equal first (fast rejection for non-anagrams), or ignoring case sensitivity and whitespace in user input
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Present both the sorting and frequency-counting solutions, analyze their time complexities, and explain when each is preferable — sorting is simpler code, frequency is faster for large character sets

sections.title: Anagram Detection Strategies
sections.content:
An **anagram** is formed by rearranging the letters of one word to form another — "listen" and "silent" are anagrams because they contain the exact same characters with the same frequencies. Checking for anagrams requires verifying that both strings have identical character composition, which can be done two ways. The **sorting approach** converts both strings to character arrays, sorts them alphabetically, then compares the sorted arrays — if they're equal, the original strings were anagrams.

Think of it like organizing two decks of cards alphabetically and checking if they match. The **frequency counting approach** builds a map of character counts from the first string, then decrements counts while iterating the second string — if all counts reach zero, it's an anagram. This is like using a tally sheet to verify matching inventory. In a backend application validating user registration (checking if username is an anagram of a blacklisted word), or in a word game service detecting valid plays, understanding both approaches and their trade-offs demonstrates **algorithmic maturity**.

The key optimization: check if lengths differ first — instant rejection saves all further processing.

sections.content:
amber|Sort approach|~normalize both|toCharArray then sort|compare the arrays|O(n log n)
blue|Count approach|~frequency match|int[26] increment for first|decrement for second|all zero means anagram, O(n)
emerald|Pre-checks|~quick reject|different length -> no|lowercase first|strip spaces
rose|Edges|~case & Unicode|"Listen" / "Silent"|ignore case and spaces?|clarify the scope

sections.title: Anagram Detection with Sorting and Frequency Counting
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use the **sorting approach** when code simplicity matters more than peak performance — it's four lines of clean code that any developer can understand and maintain. Perfect for low-frequency operations like validating username uniqueness at registration time, where the extra log factor doesn't matter.

Use **frequency counting** when performance is critical, especially for large character sets (Unicode text, long DNA sequences) or when processing many strings in a loop (batch validation of thousands of word pairs from a database). Frequency counting is O(n) versus sorting's O(n log n), which becomes significant for strings over a few hundred characters. In a real-time word game backend processing move validation, frequency counting keeps response times under 10ms. For interview settings, demonstrate both to show you understand algorithmic trade-offs. If the input can contain uppercase, lowercase, and spaces, normalize first with toLowerCase and replaceAll of spaces before checking.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping Length Check**: Freshers dive into sorting or frequency counting without first checking if the strings have the same length, wasting cycles on strings that can't possibly be anagrams ("hello" and "world" have length 5 but aren't anagrams of each other).
- **Ignoring Case and Whitespace**: Not normalizing input with toLowerCase and removing spaces, so "Listen" and "Silent" fail the check even though they're anagrams — production user input is messy.
- **Wrong Comparison Method**: Using equals on char arrays instead of Arrays dot equals, or comparing strings after sorting without converting the sorted char arrays back to strings properly.
- **HashMap Inefficiency**: Building two separate frequency maps and comparing them entry by entry instead of building one map and decrementing, which doubles the space and code complexity unnecessarily.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Definition**: Anagrams contain the exact same characters with identical frequencies, just rearranged
**Length check first**: If string lengths differ, return false immediately — saves all further computation
**Sorting approach**: Convert to char arrays, sort both, compare with Arrays.equals — O(n log n) time, simple code
**Frequency approach**: Build HashMap from first string, decrement counts for second string — O(n) time, faster for large inputs
**Space complexity**: Sorting uses O(1) extra space, frequency counting uses O(k) where k is unique characters
**Normalization**: Convert to same case with toLowerCase and remove spaces if the problem allows case-insensitive and ignores whitespace
**Trade-off**: Sorting is simpler to implement and maintain, frequency counting is asymptotically faster and better for large character sets

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To check if two strings are anagrams, I'd use one of two approaches depending on the situation. The simpler approach is sorting: convert both strings to character arrays with toCharArray, sort them using Arrays dot sort, then compare the sorted arrays with Arrays dot equals. If they're equal, the original strings were anagrams. This is O of n log n because of the sorting step, but the code is really clean — just four lines. The faster approach is frequency counting: build a HashMap from the first string counting how many times each character appears, then iterate through the second string decrementing those counts. If any count goes negative or if a character isn't in the map, they're not anagrams. If you finish and all counts are zero, they are anagrams. This is O of n time because you just iterate each string once, which is faster for long strings. The critical optimization both approaches use is checking if the lengths are equal first. If one string is length ten and the other is length twelve, they can't be anagrams, so return false immediately. That's a common mistake freshers make — they start sorting or building maps without that quick length check. Another gotcha is handling uppercase and spaces. If the problem says case-insensitive, you need to call toLowerCase on both strings first. In a production setting like checking if a new username is an anagram of a banned word, I'd use the sorting approach because it's simpler code to maintain. For high-throughput scenarios like a word game service validating thousands of moves per second, I'd use frequency counting for the speed advantage.

questions.question: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a String?
questions.title: First Non-Repeating Character
questions.direct_answer: Use a two-pass algorithm: first pass builds a HashMap of character frequencies, second pass scans the original string and returns the first character with count equal to 1. This preserves insertion order and runs in O(n) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of two-pass algorithms and HashMap usage for frequency tracking while preserving order
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Attempting a complex one-pass solution with unnecessary data structures when two simple passes are cleaner and still linear time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the int[26] array optimization for lowercase-only input (O(1) space), and briefly explain the LinkedHashMap or Stream-based queue approach as advanced alternatives

sections.title: Finding First Non-Repeating Character
sections.content:
Finding the **first non-repeating character** means identifying the earliest character in the string that appears exactly once.

The key challenge is **preserving order** — you can't just find any unique character, it must be the first one as you read left to right. A **two-pass algorithm** solves this elegantly: first pass counts how many times each character appears (building a frequency map), second pass scans the original string and returns the first character whose frequency is 1. Why two passes? Because you need to know the full count before you can decide which character is unique.

Think of it like reading a report twice — first pass highlights all recurring terms, second pass finds the first term without a highlight. This pattern appears in text processing systems analyzing log files (find the first unique error code), in user input validation (detect the first non-duplicate character in a registration code), and in data deduplication pipelines. The HashMap preserves the ability to look up any character's count in constant time, and scanning the original string ensures you find the **leftmost** unique character, not just any unique one.

sections.title: First Non-Repeating Character at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Two-pass|~count then scan|LinkedHashMap of counts|first entry with count 1|order preserved
blue|Why LinkedHashMap|~keeps insertion order|first unique is first inserted|plain HashMap loses order|return the char or -1
emerald|Array variant|~int[256] counts|first pass tallies|second pass finds count 1|O(n) time
rose|Edges|~none unique|return a sentinel like '_'|case sensitivity|empty string

sections.title: First Non-Repeating Character with HashMap
When to Use This Approach
sections.content:
Use the **two-pass HashMap solution** for general text where characters can be anything — Unicode user input, log messages with special characters, international text. This is your production default because it handles all cases correctly.

Use the **int array optimization** when input is guaranteed to be lowercase English letters only, such as processing DNA sequences (with a 4-element array for ACGT), analyzing English word puzzles, or solving constrained coding problems. The array is slightly faster and uses constant space regardless of input length. In a backend service processing user-generated content like comments or search queries, the HashMap approach is essential because you can't predict what characters appear. In an analytics pipeline counting unique letter occurrences in cleaned English text data, the array approach saves memory at scale. The two-pass strategy is actually faster in practice than attempting complex one-pass solutions with multiple data structures — two simple loops beat one complicated loop.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Iterating HashMap for Second Pass**: Freshers iterate the frequency map's keySet in the second pass instead of the original string, which loses the left-to-right order — HashMap doesn't maintain insertion order, so you'd find some unique character, but not necessarily the first one.
- **Over-Engineering One-Pass Solution**: Trying to solve this in one pass with a LinkedHashMap or Queue, which adds complexity without improving the O(n) time complexity — two simple passes are cleaner and just as fast.
- **Not Handling All-Repeating Case**: Forgetting to return null or a sentinel value when every character repeats, causing the method to return the wrong type or throw an exception.
- **Array Without Validation**: Using the int[26] array but not checking if each character is actually a lowercase letter, causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when processing strings with spaces, punctuation, or uppercase letters.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Two-pass algorithm**: First pass builds frequency map, second pass scans original string to preserve left-to-right order
**HashMap<Character, Integer>**: Stores count of each character, allows O(1) lookup during second pass
**Preserve original order**: Must scan the original string in second pass, not the HashMap's keyset, to find leftmost unique character
**Time complexity**: O(n) for both passes combined where n is string length, each pass is linear
**Space complexity**: O(k) where k is number of unique characters, or O(1) for int[26] array with lowercase letters only
**Return value**: Return the character if found, or null if all characters repeat — handle the no-result case explicitly
**Array optimization**: For lowercase a-z only, use int[26] array mapping character minus 'a' to index for O(1) space

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The cleanest solution is a two-pass algorithm using a HashMap. In the first pass, you iterate through the string and build a frequency map — a HashMap where each character is a key and its count is the value. Use getOrDefault to make that clean: map dot put c comma map dot getOrDefault c comma zero plus one. After the first pass, you know how many times each character appears. In the second pass, you iterate through the original string again, not the HashMap, and for each character you check if its count in the map equals one. The first character you find with count one is your answer. If you finish the loop without finding any, return null because all characters repeat. The key insight is why you need two passes and why you scan the original string in the second pass. You need the full frequency data before you can identify unique characters, so one pass isn't enough without complex data structures. And you must scan the original string to preserve left-to-right order — if you iterate the HashMap's keyset, you lose the order and might return some unique character that's not the first one. A common mistake freshers make is trying to solve this in one pass with a LinkedHashMap or Queue, which works but is way more complex than two simple loops that are still O of n time. For an optimization, if the input is guaranteed to be only lowercase letters, you can use an int array of size 26 instead of a HashMap. Map 'a' to index zero with character minus 'a', increment that index in the first pass, then check in the second pass. That's O of 1 space instead of O of k space where k is unique characters. In an interview, I'd present the HashMap solution as the main answer and mention the array as an optimization for constrained inputs.

questions.question: How do you remove duplicate characters from a String preserving order?
questions.title: Remove Duplicate Characters
questions.direct_answer: Use a LinkedHashSet which maintains insertion order and automatically rejects duplicates. Add each character to the set, then collect the set contents back into a String. This is O(n) time and preserves the original order of first occurrence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of LinkedHashSet's unique property of combining Set behavior with insertion-order preservation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a regular HashSet which loses order, or using StringBuilder with contains() which works but is O(n²) for large strings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the LinkedHashSet solution, explain why HashSet fails, and discuss the StringBuilder alternative with its performance trade-off — demonstrates awareness of data structure properties

sections.title: Removing Duplicates While Preserving Order
sections.content:
Removing duplicate characters while preserving order means keeping only the **first occurrence** of each character and maintaining the original left-to-right sequence. The challenge is combining two requirements: **uniqueness** (like a Set) and **order preservation** (like a List). **LinkedHashSet** is purpose-built for exactly this — it's a Set that rejects duplicates but internally maintains a linked list to remember insertion order.

Think of it like a queue at a ticket counter where each person can only enter once, but they stay in the order they first arrived. For a Java backend processing user input like cleaning up duplicate characters in search queries, or formatting display names by removing repeated letters, LinkedHashSet provides O(n) time complexity with minimal code. The alternative — StringBuilder with a contains check — works but scans the entire builder on each character, turning O(n) into O(n²) for large strings. Understanding this trade-off between data structure choice and algorithmic complexity separates developers who know Java collections from those who just use ArrayList for everything.

sections.title: Removing Duplicates with LinkedHashSet and StringBuilder
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **LinkedHashSet** for production code where correctness and performance both matter — it's the standard Java solution for this problem, O(n) time guaranteed, and any developer reading your code will immediately understand the intent. Perfect for cleaning user-generated content, removing duplicate letters from display names, or processing search query normalization in a backend service.

Use the **StringBuilder with contains** approach only in severely memory-constrained environments or when explicitly told not to use Collections — it's O(n²) time but uses slightly less memory than LinkedHashSet's internal linked list overhead. In practice, this trade-off rarely matters because modern JVMs handle small objects efficiently. For interview settings, demonstrate LinkedHashSet as your primary solution and mention StringBuilder as an alternative you'd avoid due to performance, which shows you understand algorithmic complexity. Never use a plain HashSet because it doesn't preserve order — the output would have random character sequence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using HashSet Instead of LinkedHashSet**: Freshers use regular HashSet which provides uniqueness but scrambles the order randomly, so "programming" might become "pgamin" instead of "progamin" — fails the order preservation requirement completely.
- **Not Preallocating StringBuilder**: Creating StringBuilder without specifying initial capacity when you know the maximum size (the LinkedHashSet size), causing internal array resizing and memory allocation overhead during append operations.
- **Incorrect indexOf Usage**: Using indexOf on StringBuilder with a char instead of String, or not realizing indexOf returns -1 when not found and 0 for the first position, leading to off-by-one errors in the contains check.
- **Stream Performance Ignorance**: Using fancy Stream.reduce or Stream.collect without understanding that creating intermediate strings is less efficient than simple StringBuilder append for this use case.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **LinkedHashSet**: Combines Set's uniqueness guarantee with insertion-order preservation, perfect for duplicate removal with order
**Time complexity**: O(n) for LinkedHashSet approach, O(n²) for StringBuilder with contains check
**Space complexity**: O(k) where k is unique characters, same for both approaches but LinkedHashSet has slightly higher constant factor
**HashSet fails**: Regular HashSet loses order because it uses hash codes to organize elements, not insertion sequence
**StringBuilder alternative**: Works but indexOf scans the entire builder linearly on each character, causing quadratic time
**Performance trade-off**: LinkedHashSet is faster for inputs over ~50 characters, StringBuilder with contains degrades badly on large strings
**Stream collection**: Can use stream().map(String::valueOf).collect(Collectors.joining()) but StringBuilder append is simpler

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The best way to remove duplicate characters while preserving order is using a LinkedHashSet. You create a LinkedHashSet of Character type, iterate through the string, and add each character to the set. The set automatically rejects duplicates, and because it's a LinkedHashSet, it remembers the order in which you added elements. After the loop, you iterate through the set and build a string from those characters using a StringBuilder. That gives you the deduplicated string in the original order. The whole thing runs in O of n time, which is optimal. The key is choosing LinkedHashSet instead of a regular HashSet. HashSet would give you uniqueness but the order would be random based on hash codes, so you'd lose the left-to-right sequence from the original string. LinkedHashSet maintains a doubly linked list internally to track insertion order, which is exactly what we need. There's an alternative approach using StringBuilder with a contains check — for each character, you check if it's already in the builder before appending. That works and uses less memory, but it's O of n squared time because the indexOf method has to scan the entire builder on every character. For small strings it doesn't matter, but for a thousand-character string, the LinkedHashSet approach is way faster. A common mistake freshers make is using plain HashSet and then wondering why the output is scrambled. Another is not understanding that sets in Java don't preserve order by default — only LinkedHashSet does. In a production backend service cleaning up user input or processing search terms, I'd use LinkedHashSet because it's both fast and clear to anyone reading the code what you're trying to do.
